result.topic_en: Opening draft (in Latin) of Riemann's Paris prize essay on heat conduction: it states the general problem of which conductivity properties and heat distributions keep a system of curves isothermal, sets up the general heat equation with symmetric conductivity coefficients, and plans a change of variables using a variational integral.

Quaestionem ab Ill^{ma} Academia propositam ita tractabimus, ut primum quaestionem generaliorem solvamus,
quales esse debeant proprietates corporis motum caloris determinantes & distributio caloris, ut detur systema
linearum quae semper isothermae maneant
deinde ex solutione generali hujus problematis eos casus seligemus, in quibus proprietates illae evadant ubique eaedem sive corpus sit homogeneum.

items.english: We shall treat the question proposed by the most illustrious Academy by first solving a more general question: what the properties of the body determining the motion of heat, and the distribution of heat, must be so that there exists a system of lines which always remain isothermal.

items.quote: deinde ex solutione generali hujus problematis eos casus seligemus, in quibus proprietates illae evadant ubique eaedem sive corpus sit homogeneum.
items.english: Then from the general solution of this problem we shall select those cases in which those properties become the same everywhere, i.e. the body is homogeneous.

items.quote: Disquisitionem nostram ad eum casum restringimus, in quo conductibilitas eadem est in binis directionibus oppositis
items.english: We restrict our investigation to the case in which the conductivity is the same in any two opposite directions.

items.quote:
Haec transformatio aequationis I facillime inde peti potest, quod haec
aequatio conditio est necessaria et sufficiens, ut {+designante+} [-integrale-] $\delta u$ variationem quamcunque infinite
parvam ipsius $u$ integrale
(A)
per corpus [-extensum-] tantum a valore variationis $\delta u$ in superficie pendeat.
items.english: This transformation of equation I can most easily be obtained from the fact that this equation is the necessary and sufficient condition that, δu denoting any infinitely small variation of u, the integral (A) over the body depends only on the value of the variation δu on the surface.
